newsitem.title: USA: Manufacturing growth seen slowing in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Manufacturing growth seen slowing in 1997.

text.p: Demand for cars, refrigerators and other big-ticket items will probably grow more slowly next year, restraining manufacturing output in 1997 and possibly beyond, economists said.
"It won't be a strong year for manufacturing, but it won't be as weak as 1995 or the past couple of months," said Donald Maude, chief economist at Scotia Capital Markets Inc.

Manufacturers expect revenue growth of 5.4 percent next year, according to a recent survey by industrial purchasing managers. That compares with 4.9 percent revenue growth expected for 1996 and 7.4 percent in 1995, the National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) said.
Economists said they expect factory output to be even more subdued.
Stuart Hoffman, chief economist at PNC Bank Corp., said industrial production would grow 2 percent to 2.5 percent next year, compared with about 3.8 percent so far this year.

Recent economic reports suggest output growth has slowed in the current quarter from the third quarter, largely because of growing inventories, analysts said. Output grew 0.9 percent in November, rebounding from a small drop in October.
Probably the biggest factor affecting manufacturing next year will be demand, which economists said should grow only slightly from 1996 levels.
"The demand situation out there is growth, but not runaway growth," Ralph Kauffman, chairman of NAPM's business survey committee, said in an interview last week.
Automobile manufacturing, reflecting tepid demand, might actually contract in 1997 after a good performance this year, some economists said.

"In my outlook for next year, I have consumers making fewer purchases of cars and trucks than they did this year," said PNC's Hoffman, who called for a drop of as much as 5 percent in car and light truck purchases.
"If it goes into a car or has anything to do with a car, my guess is, that sector of manufacturing will be flat to down next year," he said.

Housing probably will decline next year as well, the PNC economist said. Those two industries account for about 10 percent of manufacturing, so declines in them would weigh heavily on the industrial sector as a whole. Manufacturing overall accounts for about a fifth of the economy.

Capital expenditures are expected to fall next year, according to NAPM. Purchasing executives, on average, said they would spend 1.6 percent less on capital items in 1997, compared with a 13.5 percent increase reported for 1996.
Analysts said the planned drop in spending was probably due and may hint at slower growth for at least the next few years.
"When you have companies have an increase one year, they tend to see a smaller increase the following year," said NAPM's Kauffman, who is a professor of purchasing at the University of Houston.
Manufacturing can still grow if capital spending is cut, economists said, since cuts usually mean factory owners do not expect enough growth in production to expand capacity.
Still, a slowdown in capital spending could mean slower growth for manufacturing for the foreseesable future.
"I think it means they're looking for slower growth over the next couple of years, not just 1997," PNC's Hoffman said.
